transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2028-04-02 16:00 UTC
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Mark Chen (Palisade Head of ML), Dana Lopez (CTO), Evan Park (Finance)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Customer evaluating cost/unit tradeoffs across hosting options. Wants pilot that demonstrates predictable unit cost and headroom for load spikes. Several security and residency questions.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intro, I'm Alex, AE on infra, with Priya who is our systems SE.
[00:12] Priya: hi all, hello, i'll jump into technical levers after we cover the use case.
[00:18] Mark: Thanks. i'll give a 2 min overview - we're Palisade, we run a claims-triage LLM pipeline for insurance adjusters. Mostly ~500k tokens/day today, peaks to 2m on Mondays. We're sensitive to cost - finance put a hard cap $25k/mo for pilot.
[00:35] Dana: And security is non-negotiable, SOC2 in place, want KMS/HSM for key management, and VPC termination for private traffic.
[00:44] Alex: Ok great, helps frame it. So primary topics: unit economics and predictability, latency SLOs, and required compliance.
[01:05] Priya: quick question on the model surface - are you using a single long context generator or many short prompts?
[01:12] Mark: it's a mix. about 70% are short prompts (20-60 tokens) for classification/rerank, 30% are longer summaries (600-1,200 tokens).
[01:25] Priya: ok that distribution matters for batching and KV cache. short calls batch well, longer ones we rely on prefix caching and quantization to bring unit cost down.
[01:40] Mark: when you say prefix caching, can you explain? i.e. what are we actually saving?
[01:45] Priya: Sure. prefix/KV cache stores previous key/value activations for autoregressive models for repeated contexts—if you have repeated prefixes (like policy text, form fields), we avoid recomputing those tokens each request which can cut token compute significantly for long-context calls. We also have continuous batching windows so short requests can be combined.
[02:06] Dana: Is that compatible with private deployment? We can't send prefixes to hosted unless encrypted and under our KMS.
[02:14] Alex: Yes—Private and Dedicated modes support customer-managed KMS and audit logs. Hosted can be configured with encryption-in-transit and at-rest but for strict KMS you move to Private or Dedicated with VPC peering. There was a recent note in our security pack about that. i'll send.
[02:32] Evan: quick finance Q - how does Redwood bill batching? like if you batch 10 short requests together are we charged per output token only?
[02:41] Priya: billing is per input+output token equivalent. Batching reduces GPU overhead and thus per-token cost, but billing doesn't invent free tokens. We show net unit economics on our pricing spreadsheet—there's a difference between token billing and effective per-token compute cost after batching and cache.
[03:02] Mark: can you give a ballpark - for our mix what's a realistic per-token cost on Hosted vs Dedicated?
[03:09] Alex: ballpark: Hosted for a 13B-ish open model might be $0.0007 - $0.0012 per token raw. Dedicated with reserved capacity could be in the $0.00025 - $0.0006 range depending on commit and model optimizations. With prefix caching on long requests and heavier batching short calls, you can drop effective cost further - sometimes 30-60% improvement.
[03:36] Dana: that's a wide range. what's the main driver?
[03:39] Priya: commit level (how many GPUs/hours you reserve), model size/quantization, batching window, and how much of your workload hits the KV cache. Also whether you take burst capacity or strict SLO.
[03:52] Mark: we need 95th perc latency under 300ms for interactive adjusters. will batching break that?
[03:58] Priya: continuous batching can be tuned for latency-first settings. You can set a small batching window or use priority routes that go to low-latency nodes (dedicated). For Hosted we recommend hybrid routing: critical flows to a low-latency pool (higher unit cost) and cheaper flows to batched lanes.
[04:20] Evan: for pilot, our $25k/mo cap - what's feasible?
[04:25] Alex: rough math: if your average effective token cost is $0.0006 and you do 500k tokens/day -> ~15M tokens/mo => 15,000,000 * 0.0006 = $9,000. But peaks and longer contexts increase that. If you add redundancy, logging, and a dedicated small pool for SLO-critical traffic, you'd approach $18k-24k depending on burst settings.
[04:47] Dana: good — we want an example spreadsheet that shows three scenarios: Hosted optimized, Hosted+priority lanes, and Dedicated small pool.
[04:56] Alex: yes we'll prepare that.
[05:00] Speaker 1: (mumbled) also curious about quantization and what you support for throughput.
[05:06] Priya: we support 8-bit and mixed int quantization for certain model families; that reduces GPU memory and can give 20-40% token throughput improvement. But model quality tradeoffs need validation. We'll recommend quant profiles per model.
[05:22] Mark: are there benchmarking tools we run or you run?
[05:26] Priya: we can run a dedicated benchmark node for you with your prompt set. It simulates your distribution and gives per-token latency and cost projections. That's what we suggest for the pilot week.
[05:36] Dana: timeline — we want a 3-week pilot: week 1 benchmark, week 2 tweak configs, week 3 run production traffic shadowed. Does that fit?
[05:45] Alex: yes. we usually do a 2-4 week pilot. we'll propose the schedule in the spreadsheets.
[05:52] Evan: security questions - SOC2/ISO? can we get audit evidence?
[05:56] Alex: Redwood is SOC2 Type II; we provide attestation and an SOC pack under NDA. For Private we support customer-managed HSM/KMS and SAML SSO + RBAC.
[06:11] Dana: what about data residency? we have policies to keep EU person data in EU regions.
[06:16] Priya: we support region pinning for Dedicated/Private. Hosted also has region control but for strict residency we recommend Dedicated or Private.
[06:27] Mark: any gotchas on per-call observability? we need token-level cost breakdowns in logs.
[06:33] Alex: Redwood Console gives token-level cost per route and per model. We'll show a demo panel in the follow-up.
[06:42] Mark: ok. can you sketch an example pilot budget run?
[06:46] Alex: sure — (walkthrough) Scenario A: Hosted optimized — baseline model, default batching, no dedicated priority pool. Estimates: average effective token cost $0.0009; monthly ~13-18k for your volume. Scenario B: Hosted + priority lanes — small dedicated low-latency pool for 10% of traffic, rest batched — effective blended cost $0.0011 -> ~16-22k. Scenario C: Dedicated small pool — reserved capacity sized for your 95th perc with burst; effective token cost $0.0004 - $0.00055 -> ~10-14k plus reserved monthly. The spreadsheet will show sensitivity to KV cache hit rates.
[07:30] Priya: important note: KV cache benefits long-context calls more. If your 30% long requests reuse prefixes we can show 40-60% savings on those calls.
[07:44] Dana: our long calls are templates filled with claims history, so they should benefit.
[07:49] Mark: on the Dedicated option, what's the minimum commit?
[07:53] Alex: we can do a small reserved lane, often starting with a half-node equivalent monthly commit for pilot pricing—we'll include that in scenarios.
[08:02] Evan: and if we exceed commit with spikes?
[08:05] Priya: we offer burst to hosted pools or on-demand spillover; pricing is higher for on-demand but keeps service up. Also smart routing can fallback to a cheaper model variant if capacity is constrained.
[08:19] Dana: curious — how do you measure cache hit rate during benchmark?
[08:23] Priya: the benchmark simulates prefixes and reports KV cache hit ratio and then shows per-token compute saved. We'll give a baseline and tuned run.
[08:33] Mark: could you do a quick sketch of what the spreadsheet rows look like?
[08:37] Alex: columns: scenario, model, quant level, commit size, expected token mix, KV hit %, batching latency window, estimated tokens/mo, effective token cost, monthly estimate, caveats. We'll fill with conservative, expected, and optimistic columns.
[08:56] Mark: we will need this to go to procurement and ops. procurement will ask about termination/backout for Dedicated.
[09:03] Alex: termination terms and SLA are in the enterprise docs — we'll surface a summary and include a standard pilot amendment that allows short-term exit.
[09:12] Speaker 2: (overlap) Also, do you have any examples of customers that moved Hosted -> Dedicated and savings realized?
[09:18] Alex: yes — anonymized case where a fintech cut effective per-token cost 45% moving to Dedicated with aggressive caching and quantization plus commit. We'll summarize in the follow-up.
[09:30] Dana: for the pilot we'll likely start Hosted with a small dedicated lane — so we can avoid a heavy procurement lift.
[09:36] Priya: that is a common path: start Hosted, configure priority lanes and caching, then move to Dedicated when you see predictable run-rate.
[09:43] Mark: a few smaller points — 1) logs retention, we need 12 months for audits, 2) redaction/post-processing of PII in logs, 3) SSO integration cadence.
[09:55] Alex: logs retention & redaction are configurable; we offer retention add-ons. SSO/SAML setup usually takes 1-2 weeks. We'll include a matrix in follow-up.
[10:05] Evan: last thing — can you price out sample pilots with our $25k cap in mind? i.e. show what fits and what doesn't.
[10:12] Alex: absolutely, that's part of the three scenarios. we'll flag where you'd exceed $25k and what levers to pull (more batching, increased caching, smaller priority pool).
[10:24] Dana: great. any final technical blockers?
[10:28] Priya: only thing is we'd like sample prompts and traffic shape for the benchmark. If Mark can share a 48-hour anonymized trace with token lengths that will speed things.
[10:36] Mark: i can get that to you by EOD tomorrow, redacting personal data.
[10:40] Alex: perfect. recap of next steps: Alex sends pricing spreadsheet + pilot schedule; Priya shares KV cache docs and bench playbook; customer provides trace + success criteria; schedule bench week.
[10:54] Dana: ok thanks everyone. good session.
[10:58] Alex: thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invites and docs.

(End of transcript)
